title: Life and death questions
hook: end-of-life care and the death penalty: Christians weigh them differently, all starting from the worth of each life

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ger, the newcomer who doesn't know where the front door is. Your line was love the stranger. Who did you show one thing nobody showed you? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-five.

A woman sits in a hospital hallway with a form on her lap. Her father can't speak anymore, and the doctor has asked whether to keep every machine running. Across the city, in a courtroom, a jury is being asked a different question about a different life. Neither of these is a debate on the news for the people in those rooms. It's an ordinary day, and someone has to decide. This week has been asking who gets protected: children, the ground, the poor, every race, the stranger. Today it reaches the hardest edge of that: life and death questions.

Start with a line from the end of the Torah. Moses, in Deuteronomy, sets the choice in front of the people: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life." Christians on different sides of these debates can each appeal to that line. They disagree about what that asks. Take the end of life. The Catholic catechism, for one, draws a line. Stopping treatments that are only a burden, out of proportion to any good they can do, can be right: that's letting a dying person die in peace. Acting to end a life is something it rejects. Some other churches and individual Christians weigh assisted dying differently, and argue it out with care. Then the death penalty. Here one verse gets read two ways. Genesis 9 says, "Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man." Some Christians read the first half and hold that the state may take a murderer's life, pointing also to Paul's words that the ruler "beareth not the sword in vain." Others read the second half, the image of God, and say it's still there in the worst of us. The current Catholic catechism calls the death penalty inadmissible, and other Christians argue against it too. The answers differ. The starting point doesn't. Each side is arguing from the same root: each life is made by God, and matters to God.

Here's the practice: stand beside someone with a hard decision. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person facing a choice with no easy answer: a family deciding about care for someone they love, a friend at a crossroads, someone whose decision will change another person's life. Don't decide for them. Just keep them company in your mind. If you pray, you can use an old line from the Psalms on their behalf: "My times are in thy hand." If you don't pray, simply hold them, and wish them wisdom and peace. The bell holds the time.
Life and death questions. The hardest choices, where Christians reach different answers while starting from the same place: choose life, because each life matters to God.

Your line: every life counts. Today, when one of these questions comes up, in the news or at a table, listen for the life underneath the argument before you answer. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Christians bring these questions to prayer, pastors, chaplains and church teaching; hospital chaplains sit with families making end-of-life decisions, and churches publish statements on end-of-life care and the death penalty that reach different conclusions.

fork.setup: Moses stands before the people and sets two roads in front of them. what does he tell them to choose?
options: whatever seems best to each of them.
fork.reveal: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life." Christians on different sides of today's debates each say they are keeping that command.

original.note: Hebrew: life (a plural form), the word in "choose life" in Deuteronomy 30:19.

CCC 2278 paraphrased: discontinuing medical procedures that are burdensome, dangerous, extraordinary or disproportionate to the expected outcome can be legitimate; CCC 2277 rejects direct euthanasia. Confirm.
CCC 2267 (as revised) calls the death penalty 'inadmissible'; the script says 'the current Catholic catechism' without a date. Confirm.
'other Christians argue against it too' — stated without a count; confirm.
'Other churches and individual Christians weigh assisted dying differently' — stated without naming churches; confirm fairness.
Romans 13:4 is cited as one text some Christians use for the state's power to punish; confirm the attribution is fair.
